name: Eight Questions Before the Board Approves an AI Contract
title: Eight Questions Before the Board Approves an AI Contract
answer: This idea is a set of eight questions a school board member can ask before approving any AI contract, with written answers required before the vote. It matters because it makes risks visible before money is spent, and it turns approval into an annual review cycle rather than a single decision. If staff cannot answer the questions, the proposal is not ready and should go back for more work.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: School boards approve contracts, and AI contracts deserve extra questions. The text points to the Los Angeles chatbot that moved from launch to shutdown in a matter of months, with about $3 million paid by then. Figure 3.8 lists eight questions a board member can ask about any AI proposal, and none require technical knowledge. Each question should have a clear answer in writing before the vote. If staff cannot answer them, the proposal is not ready and the right move is to send it back for more work.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The practice sits at the board and district level, not in a specific grade band, and the text gives no grade band variations. A board member asks the eight questions from Figure 3.8 about any AI proposal. Staff must provide a clear written answer to each question before the vote. If they cannot, the board sends the proposal back for more work. Each spring, the superintendent brings an annual AI review that reports which tools are in use, what results they produced, what incidents were reported, and what they cost.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text cites EdSurge, 2024, for the Los Angeles chatbot example, which moved from launch to shutdown in a matter of months and had cost the district about $3 million by then. It also points to Figure 3.8 as the source that lists the eight questions a board member can ask. The text does not give a separate evidence label for the eight questions themselves. The finding it offers is that better questions at the start would not have prevented every problem, but they would have made the risks visible before the money was spent.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text is clear that better questions would not have prevented every problem, so the eight questions are a risk visibility tool, not a guarantee. Approval should not be the last time the board sees a tool, which is why the annual review matters. The superintendent reports tools in use, results, incidents, and costs each spring. Tools that cannot show results by the second review deserve a hard look, and some should be stopped. The decisions stay with people: the board votes, staff must answer in writing, and the board can send a proposal back or stop a tool.
